items.question: What do you see as the drawback of companies using off-the-shelf closed models when they have accumulated their own domain-specific data?
items.object: Companies using off-the-shelf closed models with proprietary domain data
items.answer: What I find very sad is that when customers use this off-the-shelf closed model, they are not leveraging all this data that they have been collecting for decades. So much data, sometimes trillions of tokens of data in a very specific domain, their domain, which is data that you would not find in the public internet. So if they are using those closed source models, they are basically not benefiting from all these insights, all these data that they have collected through years.

items.question: How do you see Voxtral TTS fitting into Mistral’s broader work on audio models?
items.object: Voxtral TTS and Mistral’s progression into speech generation
items.answer: We are releasing Voxtral TTS. It's our first audio model that generates speech. It's not our first audio model. We had a couple of releases before. We had one in the summer that was Voxtral, our first audio model, but it was a transcription model, ASR. We released some updates on top of this, supporting more languages, also features for our customers, like context biasing, diarization, timestamping in the transcription. We also had some real-time model that can transcribe audio not just at the end of the audio. You don't need to feed your entire audio file, but it can also come in real time. And here this is kind of the natural extension in audio: speech generation. So yeah, we support nine languages. This is a pretty small model, so it's very fast, very fast, and also state-of-the-art in equal performance at the same level as the best model, but it's much more efficient in terms of cost.

items.question: What do you see as the main technical novelty in Voxtral TTS?
items.object: Voxtral TTS architecture
items.answer: It's a novel architecture that we developed in-house. We iterated on several internal architectures and ended up with an autoregressive flow matching architecture, and also have a new in-house neural audio codec, which converts this audio into 1.5 Hz latent tokens, semantic and acoustic tokens. And that's the new part about this model, and they're pretty excited that it came out with such good quality.
quotes: it's a novel architecture that we developed in-house.

items.question: How do you think about the different modeling challenges in audio understanding and audio generation?
items.object: The modeling distinction between audio understanding and audio generation
items.answer:
I think there are two buckets: audio understanding and audio generation. The audio understanding, like the Voxtral models that were released earlier—Vox and Chat that were released, I think, July last year, and the follow-up transcription-only models family that were released in January—that could be one bucket, and the generation is another bucket. I think you can also treat them as a unified set of models, but currently the approaches are a little different between these two.

In the understanding model it's very similar to the Pixtral model that we also released. Voxtral was very similar in spirit. So we feed audio through an audio encoder, similar to images through a vision encoder, and it produces continuous embeddings which are fed as tokens to the main transformer decoder model. The model output is just text, so on the output side there is nothing that needs to be done in these kinds of models.

I guess the interesting part about the generation stuff is the output now has to produce audio. The approach that we have is this neural audio codec, which converts audio into these latent tokens. There's a lot of existing literature and a lot of models based off of this kind of approach, and we took slightly different design decisions around this. At the end of the day, the neural audio codec converts audio into a 12.5 hertz set of latents, and each latent has a semantic token and a set of acoustic tokens. The idea is that you take these discrete tokens and then feed them on the input side. There's several ways to fuse this at each frame, but we just sum the embeddings. It's kind of like having K different vocabularies and combining all of them because they all correspond to one audio frame on the input side.

The output side is the interesting part. On the output side, I don't know if it's the most popular, but one popular technique is to have a depth transformer because you have K tokens at each time step. Like with text, you just have one token at each time step. So you just predict the token from the vocabulary with probabilities.

items.question: Why did you choose flow matching over autoregressive prediction of the audio tokens at each time step in your audio generation model?
items.object: Flow matching for audio generation
items.answer: If you have K tokens, then the main thing would be to predict all of them in parallel, but that doesn't work. At least that doesn't work that well because audio has more entropy. One of the techniques people use is this depth transformer where you almost have a small transformer, or it can be an LSTM RNN as well, but people use transformers and you predict the K tokens in autoregressive fashion in that. So you have two autoregressive things going on. The thing we did differently is instead of having this autoregressive K-step prediction, we have a flow matching model. Instead of modeling this as a discrete token set, we train the codec to be both discrete and continuous to have this flexibility. We did try the discrete stuff, too, and it works well, but the continuous stuff works just better. So we did this flow matching. There's a flow matching head which takes the latent from the main transformer and, kind of like in diffusion, it's denoising, but in this flow matching it's a velocity estimate. So you go from this noised latent all the way to the audio latent which corresponds to the 80-ms audio, and then it's sent through the vocoder to get back the 80-ms audio frame.

items.question: How did you decide on an autoregressive transformer decoder with a flow matching head for audio generation?
items.object: Autoregressive audio generation with a flow matching head
items.answer: You can do just flow matching diffusion for the whole audio. We didn't even go down that path because one of the main applications is voice agents and we want real-time streaming, and that's the use case. That's not the only use case, but that's one of the primary use cases we want to get to. So we picked the autoregressive approach for that. Within the autoregressive space, again, you can do chunk by chunk. We picked—I think at least personally, I prefer the approaches which are the simplest, I guess. We try to see, can we just add audio as just another head to our regular transformer decoder model? Because that kind of makes it easier for eventual end-to-end modeling of audio, text-native modeling. And it works pretty well, so we kind of went with that. And we treated a little bit with the flow matching head itself. We had a discrete diffusion kind of approach, which also works well, but the flow matching one better.

items.question: Why have you chosen to develop Mistral's audio capabilities separately before combining them?
items.object: Mistral's step-by-step approach to combining audio capabilities
items.answer: So ultimately we are going to get there, but for us we decided to take it step-by-step. We start with whatever is the most important, I think also for our customers, which is transcription, the most popular use case. And then there's speech generation, the real-time just a bit before that. And then we're going to try to combine everything all together. We thought it was also important to separate things and optimize each capability one by one before we merge all of that together.

items.question: What is your intuition for why flow matching works well for speech generation?
items.object: Flow matching for speech generation
items.answer: I think the main thing is even at a particular time step, there is a distribution of things to be predicted. The way you inflect—you already know the word that you're speaking. In text space, let's say the word maps to just a single token for simplicity. In most cases, it does. So you just pick the word. But within audio, even the same word, even with your own voice, could be inflected in so many different ways. I think any approach which models this distribution well—and flow matching is one of them, it's not the only one at all, but it's the one which works pretty reasonably well. The intuition I have is there are several different clusters, each corresponding to some specific way you would inflect, pronounce that thing, and you can't predict the mean of it because that corresponds to some blurred-out speech or something like that, but you have to pick one.

items.question: How do you weigh depth transformers against flow matching for modeling speech?
items.object: Depth transformers versus flow matching for speech generation
items.answer: I think there is a lot of entropy, and modeling it as a distribution—any technique which helps with it. The depth transformer is a conditional way of modeling this, and transformers are actually good at it, but it's a mini transformer, so I think that worked pretty well for us too. It's just that the main consideration is when you have a depth transformer, if you have K tokens you need to do K autoregressive stuff. Even though it's a small thing, it's K steps, which is very big—not to say heavy—but flow matching we were able to cut it down significantly, so we are able to do inference in four steps or 16 steps, and it works pretty well. There are more normal techniques to bring it down even further, to like, in the extreme case, one step. We're not doing it yet, but at least the framework lends itself to more efficient—

items.question: How do you understand the gap between current voice models and the ability to speak to them naturally?
items.object: The gap between current voice models and natural human conversation
items.answer: What's kind of interesting in this domain is that, in a sense, if you take something simple like transcription, it doesn't seem like something that should be very hard to do for a model. It's essentially pattern recognition. It's classification. These models are very good at classifying, right? Nonetheless, when you talk to them, it's not there yet. You don't talk to them the same way you talk to a person. Maybe people don't realize it. In English, it's still much better than in any other language. Even compared to French, for instance, if you talk to this model in French, when you see people talking to this model, they will talk very slow. They will articulate as much as they can. So it's not natural, right? We are not yet to this. Maybe the next generation will not know this, but I think people that are maybe our age will actually always keep this bias of speaking very slowly when they talk to this model, even if maybe in a couple of years, maybe next year, it will not be necessary anymore. But what's interesting is to see that even for languages like French, Spanish, German that are not low-resource languages, you have a lot of audio with this, it's still not as good. I think the reason for this is just that there is not as much energy, as much effort that has been put down in some other modalities, for instance vision or coding. But there is still a lot of progress to be done. I think it's just a question of doing some work on this. There is a clear path to get there.

items.question: How do you see in-house model deployment simplifying the way companies handle sensitive data?
items.object: In-house model deployment for companies with sensitive data
items.answer: Very often they come to us for different reasons. Sometimes they have a lot of privacy concerns. They have data that is very sensitive. They don't want data to leave the company. They want it to stay inside the company. So we help them deploy models in-house, either on premise or on private cloud, so they are not worried that it's given to a third party or that there is some leakage. Many companies have different sensitivity of data. They have sometimes tier one, tier two, tier three data. Tier three can send it to the cloud; tier one can't. Then it creates some heterogeneous workflows where it's kind of annoying. You cannot send some data to the cloud, this one you can. So when we actually deploy the model for them, they don't have these considerations. They're not worried that this is going to leak. Everything is much easier. We help them do this. So it's one of the value propositions.

items.question: Why do you think companies should train models on their own data?
items.object: Training models on proprietary company data
items.answer: What's very sad is that they're not leveraging this data that they've been collecting for four years or something, for decades. So much data, sometimes trillions of tokens of data in a very specific domain, their domain, which is data that you will not find in the public internet. If they're using closed source models, they're basically not benefiting from all these insights, all this data they've collected through years. They can always give it into context at inference, but it's still not as good as if you actually train the model as is. So that's basically what we help them to do. It's basically a platform with a lot of tools to help them process data, train on that. It's actually the same thing that we're using in the science team. It's very battle-tested infrastructure, a lot of efficient training code base for continued pretraining, fine-tuning, even doing SFT well. items.question: How do you think about building tailored AI solutions for enterprise customers?
items.object: Mistral's approach to tailored enterprise models
items.answer: We have a lot of solutions. The engineers go in the company, look at the problem customers are facing, look at what they are struggling to do, what we should do to solve it. We help them solve them together. Our approach is a bit different than some of the companies and competitors. We don't just release an endpoint and say some stuff on top of that, or just give it a checkpoint. We really look very closely with customers, look at the issues they have, help them solve them, and make tailored solutions for the problems they are facing. Some examples are customers who really wanted a really good model performing on some Asian real languages. This language would be maybe 0.1% of the mixture. It has been included during training, but very, very little. What we did here is we actually trained a new model for them, where this language was 50% of the mix, which is much stronger. It knows all the dialects, it knows the slang. It's some example of things we can do, and it's really arbitrary custom. Some customers wanted a 3D model that can do audio, very good at function calling, for something in the kitchen, in the car. In particular, they wanted this to be offline because in the car you don't necessarily have access to internet. So we can build these solutions. There is no model out of the box on the internet for this. Some reasons they come to us is because they experiment with some closed source model, get some prototype, are happy with what they build, it works well, and then they want to go to production and realize it's extremely expensive. You cannot push this. Then they come back to us and say, "Can you help us build the same thing as this but using something much cheaper?" We can sometimes build something 10x cheaper by just fine-tuning a model; it will be better on prem, on their own server, and also much cheaper.

items.question: How has your understanding of the support customers need to deploy Mistral models changed since the company began?
items.object: Mistral’s strategy for helping customers deploy models
items.answer: Initially, we didn't know—I mean, we weren't competitive at the beginning of the company because I think our strategy was not exactly the same as what it is today. What we underestimated initially is the complexity of deploying this model, connecting them to everything to be sure it has access to the company knowledge. We were seeing customers struggling with this two years ago, and now things are much more complicated because now you don't just have text on the safety and simple instruction following; now you have reasoning, agents, tools, multimodal audio. items.question: How do you see the value of Mistral developing its own audio encoders?
items.object: Mistral's in-house audio encoders and real-time dual-stream architecture
items.answer: Some of the considerations in this paper were because we started with the Whisper encoder as the starting point, and now we have in-house encoders, like the real-time model we released in January. That's one nice encoder other people want to adapt. That's a good encoder, and we trained it from scratch. Now that we train encoders in-house, the design considerations are different.

items.question: How do you think about extending Mistral's text-to-speech model to hour-long audio generation?
items.object: Long-form generation in Mistral's text-to-speech model
items.answer: For the question on our text-to-speech, that also leans on the original autoregressive decoder backbone. It's almost identical considerations. The long context—and it's not even long context—the model processes audio at 12.5 Hz. So one second maps to 12.5 tokens. One minute is like 720 tokens. You can get up to 10 minutes in an 8K context window, and half an hour in a 30K context window. 32K context is something we're very comfortable training on. We can extend it much longer, 128K. So you can naturally see how it can extend to even hour-long generations. We need the data recipe and the whole algorithm to work coherently enough through such long context, but the techniques are in some way very similar to text long-context modeling. The key difference is it's just doing flow matching autoregressively instead of text-token prediction.

items.question: How do you approach bringing different capabilities together in Mistral Small?
items.object: Mistral Small’s integration of specialized capabilities
items.answer: It's a model that combines different models. Before, what we were doing is we had one model, general model for Mistral, doing instruction following with a separate model that was Destral, really for coding, specific to code. We had another model for reasoning, Magistral. These were separate artifacts built by different teams at Mistral. The way we do things internally is we have one team focused on one capability, build one model, and then once mature enough, we decide to merge this into the main picture. items.question: Why do you see open-source language models as central to Mistral's mission?
items.object: Open-source language models and Mistral's commitment to sharing science
items.answer: We've had an open source thing with us since the beginning and even before this. Before this, when I was at Meta, we released Llama. What was really nice to see was that before this, for most researchers, like universities, it wasn't possible to work on LLMs. There was no LLM outside. If you look at many of the techniques that were developed after Llama was open source, like all these post-training approaches, even DPO-type performance optimization, all of these were done by people that had access to this model, or it would have been impossible to do without this model. So it's really making us move faster. We really want to contribute to this open-source ecosystem. All these papers in the open-source community are really helping the science community as a whole to move faster. That's why we are releasing very detailed technical reports on Magistral and our first reasoning model, and publishing a lot of things that worked, things that did not work as well, etc. I think it's helpful. For the audio model, also to share a lot of details, share a lot of them for the real-time model. We really want to continue this. Basically, we belong to this community of people who share science. We really don't want to be living in a world where the smartest model, the best models, are only behind closed doors, only accessible to a company that has the power to decide who can use them. I think it's kind of a scary future we don't want to live in. We really want these models to be accessible to anyone. We want intelligence to be used and accessible by anyone that can use it. That's why we are pushing for this mission.

items.question: Why do you find Lean and formal proving valuable for training reasoning models?
items.object: Lean and formal proving as a foundation for training reasoning models
items.answer: We have a small team internally working on formal proving, formal math, a subject we care about in general. We're working on reasoning. I think we started too early before LLMs; doing reasoning without LLMs is very hard, especially when you work with formal systems, because the amount of data you have is negligible. It's a very small community of people writing formal proofs. The reason why we like it is because if you look at what people are doing with reasoning, the problems that you can use are usually going to be problems where you can verify the output. For instance, all these AIME problems where the solution is a number between 1 and 1,000, so you can compare this with a reference. Or it's an expression; you can compare the output expression generated by your model with a reference. But there are many math problems and most reasoning problems where there is no way to easily verify the solution. If the question is "show that F is continuous," you cannot compare it with a reference. If it's a proof that this is true or prove these properties, there is no way to synthetically verify the correctness of your proof. So there is no verifiable reward here. What you could provide is a judge that will look at your proof, but it's very hard and you could have some reward hacking happening there, so it's difficult. You could provide a reference proof, but then there are many ways to prove the same thing. If you give a negative reward because it's a different proof, maybe it's still a legit proof, just different. So it's not going to work well. What's nice with Lean and formal proving is that you don't have to worry about this whatsoever. They're all functional as long as they compile in Lean and functionally the same, right?

items.question: Why do you think coding agents will make software verification a much larger industry?
items.object: Software verification and the impact of coding agents
items.answer: Software verification today is a really tiny market. Very few industries work on this and need that. It's usually companies building airplanes, robotics, things where they absolutely want to be sure—life depends on this—but it's very rare that people formally verify the correctness of their software. One reason for this is simply that it's super hard to do. The reason I think people don't use it more, and why this industry is not as big as it could be, is because it is very hard. But now with coding agents, it's going to be very different. We are going to see much more of this. I think this industry is going to be much larger in the future with those theoretical models.

items.question: What do you find interesting about the connection between formal theorem proving and coding agents?
items.object: Formal theorem proving with coding agents and sub-agents
items.answer: I think in the long run, there's a lot of connection with coding agents. Sometimes a model can see a theorem that it has to prove, it's very complex. Then it can take the initiative to say, "I'm going to prove these three lemmas. I'm going to suggest three lemmas and prove each lemma in parallel with sub-agents, but I'm also going to prove the main theorem using the three lemmas." So you can do this sub-agent approach. It's pretty interesting. Even if you fail to prove one of the lemmas, you get some partial reward here. It's a bit less sparse than if you just get a zero reward for the entire thing. It's pretty interesting.
quotes: What's also interesting is not just the topic; in the long run, there's a lot of connection with coding agents.

Sometimes a model can see a theorem that it has to prove, it's very complex. Then it can take the initiative to say, "I'm going to prove these three lemmas. I'm going to suggest three lemmas and prove each lemma in parallel with sub-agents, but I'm also going to prove the main theorem using the three lemmas at home." So you can do this sub-agent approach. It's pretty interesting.

Even if you fail to prove one of the lemmas, you can actually maybe use 60 to prove the normal lemma two. So you get some partial reward here. It's a bit less sparse than if you just get a zero reward for the entire thing. It's pretty interesting.

items.question: Where do you see the research frontier in foundation model training?
items.object: Frontiers in foundation model training
items.answer: I think for us, we are still working a lot on the pretraining side. Any sort of pretraining would be a big step up compared to everything we have done before, so we are pretty excited about this. On the other side, now we have more and more to think about algorithms that will actually support these very long trajectories. Initially, you are solving math problems that can be solved in a few thousand tokens, so the model can generate them pretty quickly. When you're doing your updates, the model is never too far off. items.question: Where do you see the most promising opportunities for AI in science?
items.object: Applying AI to scientific problems through collaboration with domain experts
items.answer: We are exploring AI for science. There are a lot of areas where we think you could get extremely promising results if you apply AI in these domains. There are a lot of low-hanging fruits. You just have to find these domains where AI has not yet been applied. It's usually hard to do because the people working in these domains don't necessarily know the capability of these models. You just have to pair them with the researchers, matching with exactly what to do. But this matching we're kind of doing naturally with our customers. We have some companies we work very closely with. For instance, ISM Electronica, one of our partners. We're doing some research with them, and they have tons of extremely interesting problems in physics, science, material science that they are essentially the only ones to work on because they are doing something no one else is doing. There are many domains where AI can actually revolutionize things. You just have to think about it and be familiar with what it can do well and how to apply it. It's something we're modeling with our partners, with our customers. AI for science is very interesting.

items.question: What do you think makes someone a good forward deployed engineer?
items.object: The skills of a good forward deployed engineer
items.answer: Usually you need people that are very familiar with the tech, and not necessarily with a lot of research expertise, but that are pretty good at using this model, that know how to do fine-tuning, that know how to start an RL pipeline. It's not easy. Most customers, the majority of companies, would not be able to do this on their own. So we need people that like to solve problems, that are excited about some complex, very concrete problem. It's applied science, basically. I don't think it's too different from the skills you need in your research because essentially you are trying to find solutions to problems that customers have not yet solved. Sometimes it's easy, sometimes you have to do the work. You have to create synthetic data, find some edge cases. It depends on the problem. You need a bit of patience. Be creative. I think very similar skill sets, actually.

items.question: Why do you see Mistral’s work across many different areas as part of its value proposition to customers?
items.object: Mistral’s broad product offering and its value to customers
items.answer: We are doing many things, but I think that's also part of the value proposition. Customers are always extremely careful about their data, and they don't like trusting so many partners, trusting one partner for code, giving your data to another third party for audio and so on. They like this. What they really like with our approach is that we can help them on anything, so they don't have to send all that out to so many clouds.

items.question: How do you see the value of keeping Mistral’s research and solution teams closely connected?
items.object: Collaboration between Mistral’s research and solution teams
items.answer: In practice these two teams are still quite intertwined. Very often, first of all, they are using the same tools, the same data pipeline and everything. It's very helpful for the same team to get feedback from the solution team because they can say, "Look, these customers are trying to do this. This is not working. Can we maybe show it in the next version?"

items.question: How do you think real customer audio use cases should guide model evaluation and improvement?
items.object: Customer-specific audio evaluation and its contribution to the base model
items.answer: The real cases are just very diverse. In the specific context of a customer, you can fine-tune and make it—first evaluate, create a solid eval benchmark, and then measure in the context of their kind of audio. One use case is literally just the word for kids and they have to just say it out. It's a very specific thing. You're just saying one word and then you have to grade the kid whether they did it right, or it's like RL for kids. There are very diverse use cases and ideas. The applied scientists and engineers will go and make it better, and then from the learnings we incorporate it into the base model itself. So it's just better out of the box.
